slots.text: The real tragic hero sacrifices himself and everything that is his for the universal. Whatever he does, every emotion that stirs in him, belongs to the universal. He is disclosed, and in being disclosed he is ethics’ beloved son. That is not how it is with Abraham: he does nothing for the universal, and he is concealed.

Here, then, we have reached the paradox. Either the single individual as the single individual is able to stand in an absolute relation to the absolute — in which case the ethical is not the highest — or else Abraham is lost: he is neither a tragic hero nor an aesthetic hero.

To that extent it may again seem here that the paradox is the easiest and simplest thing of all. However, I must repeat that whoever holds himself convinced of this is not the knight of faith. For distress and anxiety are the only justification that can be thought of — even though it cannot be thought of in general terms, since then the paradox is cancelled.

Abraham keeps silent — but he cannot speak; that is where the distress and the anxiety lie. For if, when I speak, I cannot make myself understood, then I do not speak, even if I spoke without a break, night and day. This is Abraham’s case. He can say everything; but one thing he cannot say — and yet, when he cannot say it, that is, say it in such a way that another person understands it, then he does not speak. Speech brings relief because it translates me into the universal. Abraham is quite able to say the finest things any language can come up with about the way he loves Isaac. But that is not what is on his mind; what is on his mind is something deeper: that he means to sacrifice Isaac because it is a test. This last thing no one can understand, and so everyone can only misunderstand the first. This distress the tragic hero does not know. In the first place, he has the comfort that every counterargument has had its due: that he has been able to give Clytemnestra, Iphigenia, Achilles, the chorus, every living being, every voice from the heart of humanity, every cunning thought, every anxiety-provoking, every accusing, every compassionate thought, the opportunity to rise up against him. He can be sure that everything that could be said against him has been said, ruthlessly, without mercy — and to fight against the whole world is a comfort, while to fight with oneself is terrible —; he need not fear having overlooked something, so that one day, afterward, he might perhaps cry out as King Edward IV does at the news of Clarence’s murder:

Wer bat für ihn? Wer kniet' in meinem Grimm
Zu Füssen mir und bat mich überlegen?
Wer sprach von Bruderpflicht? Wer sprach von Liebe. [Who pleaded for him? Who, in my wrath, knelt / at my feet and begged me to think again? / Who spoke of a brother’s duty? Who spoke of love.]

The tragic hero does not know the terrible responsibility of solitude. Secondly, the tragic hero has this comfort: he is able to weep and lament together with Clytemnestra and Iphigenia — and while tears and cries relieve, sighs that cannot be uttered are torture. Agamemnon can quickly gather his soul into the certainty that he will act; that done, there is still time for him to comfort and encourage. Abraham cannot do this. When his heart is moved, when his words would hold a blessed comfort for the whole world, he dares not comfort; for would not Sarah, would not Eliezer, would not Isaac say to him, “Then why do you want to do it? You are free to leave it alone, after all”? And if in his distress he then wanted to give vent to his feelings, wanted to embrace everything dear to him before he went on to the final act, he might perhaps bring about the terrible thing: that Sarah, that Eliezer, that Isaac would take offense at him and believe he was a hypocrite. Speak he cannot; he speaks no human language. Even if he himself understood all the tongues of the earth, even if his loved ones understood them too, he still cannot speak — he speaks in a divine tongue; he speaks in tongues.

I can well understand this distress. I can admire Abraham. I have no fear that this story will tempt anyone to want, rashly, to be the single individual. But I also confess that I lack the courage for it, and that I would gladly renounce every prospect of getting any further, if only it were possible that I should ever, however late, get that far. At any moment Abraham can break off; he can repent the whole thing as a spiritual trial. Then he can speak, then everyone can understand him — but then he is no longer Abraham.

Abraham cannot speak; for the thing that explains everything he cannot say (that is, say so that it is intelligible): that it is a test — note carefully, a test of such a kind that the ethical is the temptation. A person placed like this is an emigrant from the sphere of the universal. But the next thing he can say even less. Abraham, as has been sufficiently shown earlier, makes two movements. In the first — the infinite movement of resignation — he gives up Isaac, and no one can understand that, since it is a private undertaking. But next, at every moment, he makes the movement of faith. This is his comfort. For he says: “Yet it will not happen; or if it does happen, the Lord will give me a new Isaac — by virtue, that is, of the absurd.” With the tragic hero, the story does at least come to an end. Iphigenia submits to her father’s decision; she herself makes the infinite movement of resignation, and now the two of them understand each other. She can understand Agamemnon, because what he undertakes expresses the universal. If, by contrast, Agamemnon were to tell her, “Even though the god demands you as a sacrifice, it could still be that he did not demand it — by virtue, that is, of the absurd,” then in that same moment he would become unintelligible to Iphigenia. If he could say it by virtue of human calculation, then Iphigenia would surely understand him; but that would imply that Agamemnon had not made the infinite movement of resignation — and in that case he is no hero; then the seer’s pronouncement is a sailor’s yarn and the whole event a vaudeville.

Abraham, then, did not speak. A single word from him is all that has come down to us: his one line to Isaac, which is itself sufficient proof that he had not spoken earlier. Isaac asks Abraham where the lamb for the burnt offering is. “And Abraham said: God will seek out for himself the lamb for the burnt offering, my son!”

This last word of Abraham’s I shall consider here a little more closely. If this word were not there, the whole event would lack something; if it were different, everything would perhaps dissolve into confusion.

I have often reflected on whether a tragic hero, whether he culminates in a suffering or in an action, ought to have a last line. As far as I can see, it depends on which sphere of life he belongs to: whether his life has intellectual significance, whether his suffering or action stands in relation to spirit.

It goes without saying that the tragic hero, in his moment of culmination, can say a few words, like any other person who has not been deprived of speech — perhaps a few fitting words. But the question is whether it is fitting for him to say them. If what his life means lies in an outward deed, he has nothing to say: whatever he says is at bottom idle talk, and it only weakens the impression he makes. Tragic ceremony requires, rather, that he fulfill his task in silence, whether it consists in an action or in a suffering. So as not to go too far afield, I will simply take what lies closest to hand. Suppose it had been Agamemnon himself, rather than Calchas, who was to draw the knife on Iphigenia: wanting to say a few words at the last moment would only have demeaned him. For the significance of his deed was, after all, plain to everyone; the procedure of piety, of compassion, of feeling, of tears was complete; and apart from that, his life stood in no relation to spirit; he was, in other words, neither a teacher nor a witness to the spirit. If, on the other hand, the significance of a hero’s life lies in the direction of spirit, then the lack of a line would weaken the impression he makes. What he then has to say is not a few fitting words, a little piece of declamation. Rather, the significance of his line is that he carries himself through at the decisive moment. Such an intellectual tragic hero ought to have the last word, and ought to keep it. One demands of him the same transfigured bearing that befits every tragic hero, but then one demands one word more. Insofar, then, as such an intellectual tragic hero culminates in a suffering (in death), he becomes immortal in this last word before he dies, whereas the ordinary tragic hero becomes immortal only after his death.

Socrates can serve as an example. He was an intellectual tragic hero. His death sentence is announced to him. In that moment he dies — for anyone who fails to see that dying takes the entire strength of the spirit, and that the hero always dies before he dies, will not get especially far in his contemplation of life. As a hero, Socrates is now required to rest calmly in himself; but as an intellectual tragic hero, he is required to have, in this last moment, strength of spirit enough to carry himself through. So he cannot, like the ordinary tragic hero, concentrate on holding his ground in the face of death. He must make this movement so quickly that in the same moment he is, in his consciousness, beyond this struggle and asserts himself. Had Socrates, then, fallen silent in the crisis of death, he would have weakened his life’s effect and raised to the suspicion that, in him, irony’s elasticity was not a world-force but a game, whose springiness at the decisive moment had to be used by the reverse measure — to hold him up with pathos.

notes.anchorAfterEn: to hold him up with pathos.
notes.text: Which line of Socrates is to be regarded as the decisive one is a matter on which opinions may differ, since in so many ways Plato has made Socrates evaporate into poetry. I propose the following. The death sentence is announced to him; at that very moment he dies, and at that very moment he overcomes death and carries himself through with his famous retort: that he was surprised to have been condemned by a majority of three votes. No loose and idle talk in the marketplace, no foolish remark by an idiot, could he have joked about more ironically than about the death sentence that condemns him — himself — to death.

slots.text: What has been briefly indicated here cannot, it is true, be applied to Abraham, if one thinks that by some analogy one could find a fitting word for Abraham to end with. It does apply, though, to the extent that one sees the necessity that Abraham must carry himself through at the last moment — that he must not draw the knife in silence but must have a word to say — for, as the father of faith, he is of absolute significance in the direction of spirit. What he is to say I can form no idea of beforehand. After he has said it, I can indeed understand — can indeed, in a certain sense, understand — Abraham in what he said, without thereby having come any closer to him than I have been in what went before. If no last line of Socrates had existed, I could have thought myself into him and formed one; and if I had not been able to do so, a poet would have managed it. But Abraham no poet can reach.

Before going on to look more closely at Abraham’s last word, I must first point out how difficult it is for Abraham to come to say anything at all. The distress and anxiety in the paradox lay, as was developed above, precisely in the silence: Abraham cannot speak. To that extent, then, it is a self-contradiction to demand that he should speak — unless one wants to have him out of the paradox again, so that at the decisive moment he suspends it, and thereby ceases to be Abraham and annuls everything that went before. If, for example, Abraham were now, at the decisive moment, to say to Isaac, “It is you this is about,” that would be only a weakness. For if he could speak at all, he would have had to speak long ago; and the weakness would then lie in his not having had the maturity of spirit and the concentration to think the whole pain through in advance. He would instead have pushed something away from himself, so that the actual pain was something more than the pain he had thought. Moreover, by speaking like this he would fall out of the paradox; and if he really wanted to speak with Isaac, he would have to turn his condition into a spiritual trial — for otherwise he could say nothing at all — and if he does this, he is not even a tragic hero.

notes.anchorAfterEn: precisely in the silence: Abraham cannot speak.
notes.text: Insofar as there can be talk of any analogy, Pythagoras’s situation at his death offers one. For he had to carry through, in his last moment, the silence he had always maintained, and therefore he said: It is better to be killed than to speak. Cf. Diogenes, Book 8, § 39.

slots.text: Nevertheless, a last word of Abraham’s has been preserved; and to the extent that I can understand the paradox, I can also understand how Abraham is totally present in this word. First and foremost, he says nothing, and it is in this form that he says what he has to say. His answer to Isaac is ironic in form; for it is always irony when I say something and yet do not say anything. Isaac asks Abraham on the assumption that Abraham knows. Now, if Abraham had answered, “I know nothing,” he would have said an untruth. To say something is beyond him; for what he knows, he cannot say. So he answers: “God will seek out for himself the lamb for the burnt offering, my son!” From this one sees the double movement in Abraham’s soul, as it has been described in what went before. Had Abraham merely given Isaac up in resignation and done no more, then he would have said an untruth; for he knows perfectly well that God demands Isaac as a sacrifice, and knows that he is himself ready, at this very moment, to sacrifice him. So at every moment, after making this movement, he has made the next one: he has made the movement of faith by virtue of the absurd. To that extent he says nothing untrue; for by virtue of the absurd it is, after all, possible that God could do something entirely different. So he says nothing untrue — but neither does he say anything; for he speaks in a foreign tongue. That becomes clearer still once we remember that the one who was to sacrifice Isaac was Abraham himself. Suppose the task had been different: suppose the Lord had ordered Abraham to take Isaac out to Mount Moriah, and had then let his own lightning strike Isaac and taken him as a sacrifice that way. In that case Abraham would, in a straightforward sense, have been right to speak as enigmatically as he does; for then he himself could not know what would happen. But as the task is set for Abraham, he himself must act. So at the decisive moment he must know what he himself will do, and so he must know that Isaac is to be sacrificed. If he has not been certain of this, he has not made the infinite movement of resignation; and in that case, though his word is certainly no untruth, he is also very far from being Abraham: he is of less account than a tragic hero; indeed, he is an irresolute man who can make up his mind neither to the one thing nor to the other, and who for that reason will always end up speaking in riddles. But such a hesitator is the very parody of the knight of faith.

So it appears here again that one can indeed understand Abraham, but only understand him in the way one understands the paradox. For my part, I can indeed understand Abraham, but I also comprehend that I do not have the courage to speak like that, any more than I have the courage to act like Abraham. Yet I by no means say, on that account, that it is something slight; on the contrary, it is the one thing that is wondrous.

And what, then, did his own age judge of the tragic hero? That he was great — and it admired him. And that honorable assembly of the noble, the jury that every generation sets up to judge the generation that has gone before, judged the same. But Abraham there was no one who could understand. And yet what did he attain? That he stayed true to his love. But a person who loves God needs neither tears nor admiration: he forgets the suffering in his love. Indeed, he has forgotten it so completely that afterward there would not be the slightest trace of a notion of his pain, were it not that God himself remembered it — for God sees in secret, and he knows the distress and counts the tears and forgets nothing.
Either, then, there is a paradox — that the single individual as the single individual stands in an absolute relation to the absolute — or Abraham is lost.
